items.readable_text:
Content:
Measuring means finding a number that describes the size of something. In particular, we determine the duration between two events by measuring the time between those events. We use time units for this purpose.

Content:
The most popular measurement system within the scientific community is the metric system. Within the metric system, the most common units of measurement are called base units.

Content:
The base unit for time is the second, which we denote using the symbol "[MATH: \textrm{s}.]" We measure the time between two events using clocks like the ones shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8687103d44c00097a2bde24396e78096]

Content:
We use milliseconds to measure smaller time intervals. The symbol for milliseconds is "[MATH: \textrm{ms}.]" The prefix [MATH: \textrm m] stands for milli, which means [MATH: \dfrac{1}{1\,000}.] Therefore, [MATH: 1\,\textrm{ms}] equals [MATH: \dfrac{1}{1\,000}\,\textrm s.]

Content:
Notice that if we add [MATH: 1\,\textrm{ms}] to itself [MATH: 1\,000] times, we get exactly [MATH: 1\,\textrm{s}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 1ms + 1ms + ⋯ + 1ms^(⏞)^(1000times)|=; (1)/(1000)s + (1)/(1000)s + ⋯ + (1)/(1000)s|=; 1000 × (1)/(1000)s|=; (1000 × 1)/(1000)s|=; (1000)/(1000)s|=; 1s]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 1\,000\,\textrm{ms}] equals [MATH: 1\,\textrm{s},] as stated in the diagram.

Content:
One millisecond is a very short time interval. To put this into context, a single blink of a human eye is around [MATH: 200] milliseconds on average.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Measuring means finding a number that describes the size of something. In particular, we determine the duration between two events by measuring the time between those events. We use time units for this purpose.

Content:
The most popular measurement system within the scientific community is the metric system. Within the metric system, the most common units of measurement are called base units.

Content:
The base unit for time is the second, which we denote using the symbol "[MATH: \textrm{s}.]" We measure the time between two events using clocks like the ones shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8687103d44c00097a2bde24396e78096]

Content:
We use milliseconds to measure smaller time intervals. The symbol for milliseconds is "[MATH: \textrm{ms}.]" The prefix [MATH: \textrm m] stands for milli, which means [MATH: \dfrac{1}{1\,000}.] Therefore, [MATH: 1\,\textrm{ms}] equals [MATH: \dfrac{1}{1\,000}\,\textrm s.]

Content:
Notice that if we add [MATH: 1\,\textrm{ms}] to itself [MATH: 1\,000] times, we get exactly [MATH: 1\,\textrm{s}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 1ms + 1ms + ⋯ + 1ms^(⏞)^(1000times)|=; (1)/(1000)s + (1)/(1000)s + ⋯ + (1)/(1000)s|=; 1000 × (1)/(1000)s|=; (1000 × 1)/(1000)s|=; (1000)/(1000)s|=; 1s]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 1\,000\,\textrm{ms}] equals [MATH: 1\,\textrm{s},] as stated in the diagram.

Content:
One millisecond is a very short time interval. To put this into context, a single blink of a human eye is around [MATH: 200] milliseconds on average.
